steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: More rain will probably fall in September than in July.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In the past two years, significantly more rain has fallen in September than in July.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This isn't a crazy argument. The author is assuming that what happened in the recent past will probably happen again in the near future.

Given that September beat July in each of the last two years, how could we argue that July might still get more rain this year? Easily. Two years is a tiny record. Two seasons can line up that way by chance, the way a fair coin can land heads twice in a row. And maybe something about this year is different from the last two.

Notice that the author was careful: the conclusion says "probably," not "definitely." That softer wording helps, but it doesn't save the argument. Even "probably" needs more than two data points behind it. The flaw is the size of the record, not the strength of the claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the prediction rests on too few past cases: two years is not enough to say what this year will do. An answer could also say the author overlooks that this year may differ in some important way from the previous two. Expect abstract wording, so be ready to translate "future event" and "instances of related past events" back into this year's rain and the last two years.

notes.body: Circular reasoning means the premise already assumes the conclusion, so the argument proves nothing new. Here the premise is about the last two years and the conclusion is about this year. Those are different claims: the premise could be true and this year could still go the other way. The evidence is thin, but it is real evidence.

Translate the abstract words back into the argument. The phrase "an inference about a future event" is the prediction about this year's rain. The phrase "a very limited number of instances of related past events" is the two previous years. That matches our prediction exactly: two years is too small a record to support even a "probably" about this year.

The move to repeat: when an argument predicts the future from the past, count the past cases. If there are only a handful, look for an answer about a small or limited sample, often worded abstractly like this one.

The argument never mentions averages or one unusually wet year, so it can't overemphasize that possibility. It doesn't raise it at all. If anything, a critic would say the author ignores how one strange year could distort a two-year record. C describes the opposite of what the author does.

D describes concluding that two things are linked because they often show up together. The author doesn't conclude that anything is associated; the conclusion is a prediction about this year. And D's "many instances" gets the evidence backwards: the problem here is that there are only two.

The argument cites no source at all. The rainfall in the previous two years is stated as a premise, and on Flaw questions we accept premises as true. Even with perfect rainfall records, two years would still be too few, so reliability isn't the problem.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
old_steps.body: More rain will probably fall in September than in July.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: In the past two years, significantly more rain has fallen in September than in July.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This isn't a crazy sounding argument. The author is assuming that what's been true in the recent past will probably be true in the near future. For example, "For the past two Christmas's, my neighbor has put a big snowflake over her front door. Therefore, this year she will probably hang a big snowflake over her front door." We know that "just because it was true in past instances, it doesn't have to necessarily be true again in this instance." This argument is more responsible. It's only predicting that it will probably happen again in this instance. But that's still potentially an exaggeration. Maybe something was different about the last two years from this coming year.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer mentioning the "if it was true before, it'll probably be true again" reasoning move, or an answer pointing out the "maybe this year is importantly different from the previous two years" objection.

old_notes.body: Circular reasoning occurs when a premise already contains or presupposes the conclusion, such that the argument essentially proves itself by assuming what it set out to demonstrate. That is not what happens here. The premise — that September had more rain than July in the previous two years — is a factual observation about past events. The conclusion — that September will probably have more rain than July this year — is a prediction about the future. These are logically distinct claims: one is about what has already happened, the other about what will happen. The premise does not secretly assume the conclusion; it just provides inadequate evidence for it. The problem is insufficient data, not self-referential logic.

The argument observes a pattern over just two years and uses it to predict what will happen this year. Two instances is an extremely limited basis for drawing any general conclusion, let alone a prediction about future weather. Rainfall patterns can vary dramatically from year to year due to shifting weather systems, El Nino cycles, and countless other variables. The fact that September outpaced July for two consecutive years could easily be coincidental rather than indicative of any underlying trend. The argument treats this tiny sample as though it reveals a reliable pattern, when in reality it reveals almost nothing about what to expect going forward. This answer correctly identifies the core vulnerability: the inference about the future rests on far too few past observations to carry any real predictive weight.

The argument does not discuss average rainfall statistics, nor does it rely on averages that could be distorted by outlier events. The evidence is simply that September had more rain than July in each of the previous two years. The concern about large storms skewing averages is a valid statistical consideration in other contexts, but it does not describe what is happening in this argument. The argument's problem is not that its data might be distorted by outliers; the problem is that there are only two data points in the first place. Even if each year's rainfall figures were perfectly representative and undistorted, two years would still be too few to support a predictive conclusion. This answer addresses a statistical concern that is not relevant to the argument's actual flaw.

This answer describes a flaw in which someone observes that two things often co-occur and concludes they are associated. But the argument here is not about the association between two phenomena — it is about predicting future rainfall based on past rainfall. The argument does not claim that September and heavy rain are "associated" in some general sense; it observes a specific pattern over two years and predicts that pattern will continue. Additionally, this answer mentions "many instances," which mischaracterizes the evidence. The argument relies on only two instances, which is precisely the problem. The flaw described here — correlating co-occurrence with association from many observations — simply does not match the structure of this argument.

The argument does not rely on evidence from a source whose reliability is questionable. It simply states a factual claim about rainfall in the previous two years. There is no cited study, no unnamed expert, no secondhand report — just a direct observation about how much rain fell. The argument's problem has nothing to do with the trustworthiness of its evidence source and everything to do with the quantity of evidence. Even if the two-year rainfall data were obtained from the most reliable meteorological instruments on Earth, two years would still be too few data points to support a weather prediction. This answer raises a concern about evidence reliability that is simply not at issue in the argument.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: There are exceptions to the general rule that people should practice what they preach. Rephrase: sometimes it's fine for people not to act the way they tell others to act.

steps.label: Evidence (for instance)
steps.body: Logicians don't need to be logical in their discussions of logic, any more than physicians need healthy lifestyles in order to treat people.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author's example of an exception is an analogy. Physicians preach health, and nobody thinks a physician has to live a healthy life to treat patients well. So, says the author, logicians don't have to be logical in their discussions of logic either.

Any time an argument rests on an analogy, ask: are these two cases alike in the way that matters? The physician case works. A physician's lifestyle happens outside the job. A physician who never exercises can still diagnose and prescribe correctly.

The logician case is different. Being logical while discussing logic isn't something a logician does after work. It is the work. A logician who argues illogically about logic is doing the job badly. How would anyone come away understanding logic if the lesson itself were illogical?

So, given the physician example, how could we argue the logician example still fails? Point out that the physician's failure is personal, while the logician's failure is professional.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that breaks the analogy: being illogical in discussions of logic is a failure at the logician's actual job, while an unhealthy lifestyle doesn't stop a physician from treating people well. The stem says "fails to take into account," so the right answer will be a fact that, had the author considered it, would weaken the comparison.

notes.body:
This is the broken analogy we predicted. A logician who is illogical in discussions of logic is failing at the core of the job, which is incompetence. A physician with an unhealthy lifestyle can still treat people well. So the two cases aren't alike in the way the argument needs.

Run the stem's test. The phrase "fails to take into account" means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. It does. If the logician's failure is incompetence and the physician's isn't, the physician example can't earn logicians the same pass.

The move to repeat: on an analogy argument, the right Flaw answer usually names the relevant difference between the two cases.

B is about a physician whose health "deteriorates badly," not one with an unhealthy lifestyle, which is what the argument discusses. And at most B questions the physician half of the analogy, which is the half that works. It says nothing about whether a logician must be logical when discussing logic.

The argument is about what each profession needs to do, not about which one causes more harm. Incompetent physicians could be far more dangerous than illogical logicians, and the question of whether logicians must be logical about logic would be untouched.

How hard a standard is to meet doesn't decide whether it is required. Something can be very difficult and still be necessary for doing a job well. D compares difficulty, while the argument is about necessity, so it misses the flaw.

E agrees with the author: it accepts that logicians don't need to be logical to be competent at discussing logic. Calling it "highly desirable" doesn't contradict the claim that it isn't necessary. A Flaw answer has to hurt the argument, and an answer that concedes the author's point can't be what the author failed to account for.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: There are exceptions to the general rule that you should practice what you preach. rephrase: Sometimes its okay if you don't act in accordance with what they say.

old_steps.label: Evidence (for instance)
old_steps.body: Logicians don't need to be logical when they discuss logic, just like physicians don't have to be healthy to discuss health.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The author is trying to support the idea that sometimes it's okay if you don't practice what you preach. The evidence is an analogy, in which the author is assuming in both cases that it's okay if you don't practice what you preach. It's okay for a doctor to tell her patient to stop smoking cigarettes, even though she herself hasn't been able to quit smoking. It's okay for a logician to be discussing logic, even though they are being illogical as they do so. Any time an argument is based on an Analogy, we should be asking ourselves whether the two things feel fair to compare. In this case, it does seem perfectly fine for a doctor to treat my health conditions, even if they don't live a healthy lifestyle. But it doesn't seem as fine for a logician to be illogical while discussing logic. How will I emerge with a better understanding of logic, if the logician teaches it to me in some illogically? To put it another way, what a physician does outside her clinic to her own body doesn't really affect how she treats people inside her clinic. The former is her life. The latter is her job. But what a logician does within a discussion of logic seems like it is his job, not his life. If he can't be logical while discussing logic, then he's messing up being a logician.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer complaining about the analogy, probably regarding the fact that while the physician example works for "you don't need to practice what you preach", the logician example seems weirder.

old_notes.body: This answer identifies the critical disanalogy that undermines the argument. The argument treats two cases as parallel exceptions to "practice what you preach," but they are fundamentally different. A logician who is illogical in discussions of logic is failing at the core competency of their profession. Logic is not just what logicians preach — it is the tool they must use to do their work. Being illogical when discussing logic means being incompetent at the very activity that defines the profession. By contrast, a physician's personal lifestyle is separate from their professional competence. A doctor who smokes, overeats, or never exercises can still diagnose diseases, perform surgery, and prescribe effective treatments. The physician's failure to practice what they preach involves personal behavior, not professional skill. The argument treats these as equivalent exceptions, but one involves professional incompetence while the other involves a personal shortcoming that does not affect job performance. This disanalogy destroys the argument's reasoning.

This answer raises a scenario where a physician's health deterioration might prevent them from treating patients. While this is true in extreme cases, it does not identify the argument's actual flaw. The argument's problem is not that unhealthy physicians might eventually become too sick to work — it is that the comparison between logicians and physicians is fundamentally flawed from the start. Even a physician in perfect enough health to practice medicine can have unhealthy habits without being professionally incompetent, whereas a logician who is illogical in logical discussions is incompetent by definition. This answer addresses a peripheral concern about the physician example rather than identifying the core disanalogy between the two cases.

The argument is not about the relative harm that incompetent professionals might cause. Whether incompetent physicians cause more harm than incompetent logicians is irrelevant to whether the two cases are proper exceptions to "practice what you preach." The argument's flaw is that it treats two structurally different situations as equivalent: one where the gap between preaching and practice constitutes incompetence (logicians), and one where it does not (physicians). Comparing the severity of harm from incompetence in each profession is a completely different conversation that does not touch the argument's actual reasoning error. The issue is whether the analogy holds, not which profession poses greater risks when things go wrong.

The relative difficulty of becoming logical versus adopting a healthy lifestyle does not address the argument's flaw. The argument fails because it treats two structurally different cases as analogous: a logician being illogical in discussions of logic is a case of professional incompetence, while a physician having an unhealthy lifestyle is a personal shortcoming separate from professional skill. How hard it is to achieve either standard is irrelevant to whether the two situations are properly analogous. Even if becoming logical were the easiest thing in the world, the argument would still fail because the analogy compares two fundamentally different types of "not practicing what you preach." Difficulty is beside the point when the core issue is the nature of the gap between preaching and practice.

This answer concedes the argument's claim about logicians and then adds that being logical is still "desirable." But the argument's flaw is not that being logical is merely desirable rather than necessary — the flaw is that the analogy between logicians and physicians is broken. The argument treats the logician case as equivalent to the physician case, when in fact a logician who is illogical in logical discussions is professionally incompetent, while a physician with an unhealthy lifestyle is not. This answer essentially agrees with the argument's framing (logicians need not be logical to be competent) and adds a minor qualification, missing the fundamental problem with the comparison entirely.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: My paper wasn't graded in accordance with the professor's stated criteria.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The professor said A's would go only to papers whose conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. My conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence, and the professor admits it, but my paper got a B.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
When a Flaw stimulus contains conditional logic, suspect the most common famous flaw: Necessary vs. Sufficient. The author takes a rule and runs it backward or negates it.

"Only" introduces a necessary condition. So the professor's rule is:

gets an A → conclusions supported by reliable statistical evidence

That rule says reliable evidence is required for an A. It doesn't say reliable evidence earns an A. The student reasons: my paper had reliable evidence, so it should have gotten an A. That is the reversal. It treats a requirement as a guarantee.

An everyday version: "Only people with a ticket get into the concert." Having a ticket doesn't promise entry. You could still be turned away for showing up after the doors close. The professor may have other requirements too, like clear writing or a sound argument, and the paper may have missed one of them. A B is perfectly consistent with the stated rule.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer calling out the formal Necessary vs. Sufficient error: the student treats something required for an A as if it were enough for an A. An answer could also say the student fails to consider that there may be other requirements for an A besides well-supported conclusions.

notes.body: A accuses the student of a motive: bringing up the criteria to distract from the paper's weaknesses. Nothing in the argument tells us why the student is complaining. The flaw is in how the student reads the rule, and that flaw would be there whatever the motive.

B describes drawing a value judgment from facts alone. But the student's conclusion isn't really a value judgment: whether the paper was graded by the professor's stated criteria is a question of fact about what the rule says and what grade was given. The student's facts are fine. The error is treating a requirement for an A as if it guaranteed an A.

This is the reversal we predicted, in abstract words. The phrase "a condition that is among the requirements for a particular grade" is reliable statistical evidence, which the word "only" makes required for an A. The phrase "a condition that is enough to guarantee that grade" is how the student treats it: I had reliable evidence, so I deserved an A.

The move to repeat: when a Flaw stimulus has "only," "only if," "requires," or "must," diagram it, then check which side the author treats as the trigger. If the author uses the necessary side to prove the sufficient side, the answer will say the argument confuses what is required with what is enough. The test can word that many ways: "necessary" vs. "sufficient," "required" vs. "guarantee," or, as here, "among the requirements" vs. "enough."

D says the argument rests on a biased report. But the key fact isn't the student's word alone: the professor acknowledges that the conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. And a neutral observer making this exact argument would commit the same error, so bias isn't the flaw.

The student's conclusion is about the professor's stated criteria, not about some objective standard of quality. The argument never brings up objective criteria, so it has no need to distinguish them. The flaw is a misreading of the professor's own rule.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: My paper wasn't graded in accordance with the professor's stated criteria.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The professor said that she would only give A's to papers whose conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. My conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence, but I got a B.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Whenever we're dong Flaw and we see conditional logic (only), we immediately suspect we're dealing with the #1 Famous Flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author provides a conditional logic rule but thinks about the rule in the style of an illegal negation or reversal. The word "only / only if" always signifies a necessary condition, so the rule the professor gave is this:
```
Give A → Conc supported w/ good evidence
```
    An illegal negation would sound like this: "My paper didn't get an A. Thus, its conclusions must not have been supported with good evidence." An illegal reversal would sound like this: "My conclusions were supported with good evidence. Thus, my paper will get an A." And that's just what the author did. He is thinking that having well supported conclusions is sufficient, like as long as he had well supported conclusion he should be getting an A. But the professor said that well supported conclusion were required, not that they were all you need. There might be other requirements too. For example the professor might say, "I go on dates only with men who are at least 5' 8" in height." Does that mean that the professor is going to be willing to go on a date with every single man whose 5'8" or taller? Of course not. She's saying that's a requirement, not a guarantee.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Let's look for something calling out the formal Necessary vs. Sufficient error, or look for an answer otherwise saying that the students is failing to consider that there might be other benchmarks you need to hit to get an A, in addition to just having well supported conclusions.

old_notes.body: The student is not using the grading criteria as a distraction from the paper's shortcomings. The student genuinely believes the criteria were violated and is making a logical argument — albeit a flawed one — to support that belief. "Drawing attention away from shortcomings" describes a rhetorical tactic of deliberate misdirection, but the student's error is logical, not rhetorical. The student sincerely misunderstands the logical structure of the professor's criteria, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. There is no evidence of intentional deflection or strategic manipulation. The flaw is in the reasoning, not in the motives behind the reasoning.

Drawing evaluative conclusions from factual claims is not inherently flawed — it is how most arguments work. The student observes factual conditions (the professor's stated criteria, the paper's characteristics, and the grade received) and draws an evaluative conclusion (the grading was inconsistent). The problem is not the type of conclusion drawn but the logical error in getting there. The student treats a necessary condition as sufficient, which is a specific structural flaw in the reasoning. This answer describes a general argumentative pattern (facts leading to evaluations) that is perfectly legitimate in most contexts and does not identify the specific logical error that makes this particular argument flawed.

This answer precisely identifies the student's logical error. The professor said she would give A's "only to" papers with reliable statistical evidence. The word "only" establishes a necessary condition: you need reliable statistical evidence to get an A. It does not establish a sufficient condition: having reliable statistical evidence does not guarantee you an A. The student takes this necessary condition — one requirement among potentially many — and treats it as a sufficient condition, assuming that meeting it alone should produce an A. But the professor could have additional unstated criteria: quality of writing, depth of analysis, originality, methodological rigor, or any number of other standards. The student's paper met one necessary condition while potentially failing others, making the B grade perfectly consistent with the stated criteria. The student's complaint is built entirely on a logical confusion between what is required and what is enough.

The student is a participant in the controversy, but calling the report "biased" does not identify the logical flaw in the argument. Even if we grant that the student has a personal stake in the outcome, the argument's flaw is structural, not motivational. The student's reasoning would be equally flawed if a disinterested third party made the exact same argument. The necessary-sufficient confusion exists regardless of who makes it. Additionally, dismissing an argument solely because the arguer has a personal interest is itself an ad hominem approach. The student could be biased and still correct, or biased and logically wrong — but the wrongness comes from the logic, not the bias.

The distinction between the professor's subjective grading criteria and some external "objective criteria for evaluating papers" is not relevant to the student's logical error. The professor announced her criteria and graded accordingly; whether those criteria are objective or subjective is a separate issue entirely. The student's argument fails because it confuses a necessary condition for an A (reliable statistical evidence is required) with a sufficient condition (reliable statistical evidence is all that is needed). This confusion exists whether the criteria are perfectly objective, entirely subjective, or some combination. The philosophical nature of the grading standards has no bearing on the structural flaw in the student's reasoning.

steps.label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
steps.body: The company acted fairly in failing to give bonuses to the staff.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Some people claim the company was unfair, perhaps because they recall that the company promised that if profits were higher than last year's, the staff would get bonuses.
But profits were much smaller than last year's.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Lindsey is rebutting an opposing position. Some people say the company was unfair. Lindsey guesses at their reason ("Perhaps"): the company's promise that the staff would all get bonuses if profits increased over last year's. Then Lindsey knocks that reason down. The promise was:

profits increase over last year's → staff all get bonuses

Profits were much smaller than last year's, so the promise never kicked in, and it didn't require bonuses. Fair enough. But Lindsey concludes much more: the company acted fairly.

Given that the promise didn't require bonuses, how could we argue the company still acted unfairly? Easily. Maybe the staff worked unpaid overtime all year. Maybe executives paid themselves large bonuses while the staff got nothing. The critics may have had reasons Lindsey never mentions.

This is the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw. Defeating one argument for a claim doesn't prove the claim false. Example: "Some people say this restaurant is bad, perhaps because the parking is terrible. But the lot was just doubled in size. Clearly the restaurant is good." The food could still be awful.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying Lindsey concludes a claim is false just because one possible reason for it fails. An answer might also point out that Lindsey only guesses at the critics' reason ("Perhaps") rather than answering the reasons they actually gave.

notes.body: Lindsey doesn't rely on the critics' opinions; Lindsey argues against them. Whether those unnamed people were well informed doesn't matter to the reasoning, because their view is never used as evidence. A describes building a case on someone's opinion, which is the reverse of what happens here.

This matches the prediction. In B, "an opinion" is the claim that the company was unfair. The phrase "one potential reason for that opinion" is the bonus promise, which Lindsey only guesses the critics had in mind. And "has been undermined" is the point that profits fell, so the promise never required bonuses. From that alone, Lindsey infers the opinion is false and the company was fair.

The word "merely" carries the criticism: one failed reason isn't enough to prove the opposite. The move to repeat: when an author attacks an opponent's reason and then concludes the opponent's claim is false, look for Unproven vs. Proven False. Showing that a reason fails leaves the claim unproven, not disproven.

C describes an attack on the people: dismissing a claim because of who made it. Lindsey says nothing about the critics' character, motives, or qualifications. Lindsey goes after a reason for their claim, the bonus promise, so the attack is on an argument, not on people.

D is tempting because the argument is about profits. But there's no confusion. The promise was about an increase over last year's profits, and Lindsey compares this year's profit to last year's, which is exactly the right comparison. A profit much smaller than last year's is not an increase. The math is fine; the error is the leap from one failed reason to the claim that the company acted fairly.

Run the test: "overlooks the possibility" means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. E says a policy can be fair without being generous. That helps Lindsey, who argues the company was fair even though it paid no bonuses. An idea that supports the conclusion can't be what the author failed to consider.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
old_steps.body: The company acted fairly in failing to give bonuses to the staff.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body:
Some people claim the company was unfair, perhaps because they recall that the company promised that if profits were higher than last year's, the staff would get bonuses.
But profits were much smaller than last year's.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and the author is rebutting some other position and concluding the polar opposite position, we want to be thinking about the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw.
EXAMPLE - Some people claim that cell phones cause cancer. But no scientific study has ever determined this. Thus, cell phones do not cause cancer.
The flaw here is that even though someone else failed to prove that cell phones DO cause cancer, that doesn't mean the author has presented any evidence that proves cell phones DON'T cause cancer.
In this argument, some people claim "the company acted unfairly" in failing to give the staff bonuses. Our author ends up concluding "the company acted fairly", and this is not by presenting positive evidence of her own in favor of this conclusion.
Instead, she's just taking down the argument that (she thinks) was being made in favor of the opposite conclusion.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body:
The author should be responding to the actual reasons these several people offered in defense of their claim that the company was unfair, not speculating that "Perhaps they were basing their claim on X". So an answer might complain about that.
Even if the author is correct, and the people were basing their argument on X, the fact that the author has shown that X is not a valid way to prove "Unfair" doesn't suddenly mean that the author has proven "Fair". This is more in the Unproven vs. Proven False vein.

old_notes.body: This answer describes a flaw involving reliance on unnamed or poorly informed authorities. But Lindsey does not rely on unnamed sources to build her OWN case — she responds to other people's complaint by challenging their reasoning. The issue is not WHO is making the complaint or whether they are well-informed. The issue is HOW Lindsey responds to the complaint. She defeats one reason for the opinion and concludes the opinion is false. The flaw is structural (incomplete refutation), not epistemic (unreliable sources). Even if the complainers were perfectly informed experts, Lindsey's logical error would be identical.

This answer precisely identifies Lindsey's logical error. People claimed the company's decision was unfair, and one supporting reason was that the company had large profits (or profits had increased). Lindsey showed that this particular reason is factually weak — profits were actually smaller. So far, so good. But then she makes the leap: since this one reason is undermined, the entire opinion must be wrong, and the company acted fairly.

This is a textbook incomplete refutation. An opinion can rest on multiple independent reasons. The employees might believe the decision was unfair because of contractual promises, precedent, management compensation, industry norms, or other factors Lindsey never addresses. By treating one challenged reason as the entire foundation for the opinion, Lindsey dramatically overstates what her evidence accomplishes. She refuted one premise and concluded she had refuted the conclusion — but conclusions can survive the loss of a single supporting reason if other reasons remain intact.

This answer describes an ad hominem fallacy — dismissing a claim by attacking the character or attributes of the people making it rather than addressing the substance. But Lindsey does not attack the complainers personally. She does not question their intelligence, motives, credibility, or character. Instead, she directly engages with one factual claim they rely on (the profit level) and attempts to refute it. Lindsey's flaw is different: she engages with the substance but treats her rebuttal of one supporting reason as a complete refutation of the opinion. She deserves credit for engaging with the argument — she just does so in a logically incomplete way.

This answer accuses Lindsey of confusing the size of profits with the amount by which profits increased — conflating absolute levels with rates of change. But Lindsey does not make this mathematical error. Her argument about profits is straightforward: people thought profits were large (or had increased), and Lindsey points out that profits were actually much smaller. She does not mix up "total profits" with "profit growth." Her error lies elsewhere — in the logical leap from "one reason for the opinion is wrong" to "the opinion itself is wrong." This answer identifies a mathematical confusion that is not present in the argument.

This answer suggests Lindsey conflates fairness with generosity — perhaps arguing the company was fair when the real issue is that it was not generous. But Lindsey does not slide between these concepts. She directly argues the company's decision was fair, and the complainers directly argue it was unfair. Neither side introduces or confuses the concept of generosity. Lindsey's actual flaw is structural: she shows one reason for the unfairness claim is wrong and leaps to the conclusion that the company acted fairly. This is an incomplete refutation error, not a semantic confusion between "fair" and "generous." The flaw described in this answer simply is not present in Lindsey's reasoning.

steps.label: Conclusion (probably)
steps.body: Making some stuff from recycled materials is probably as bad for the environment as it would be to make it from nonrecycled materials.

steps.label: Evidence (and)
steps.body: The recycling process for those products uses as much energy as producing them from raw materials, and almost all energy production damages the environment.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Given that recycling these products uses as much energy as producing them from raw materials, how can we argue that making them from recycled materials is still better for the environment?

One route would be to say the energy used for recycling is cleaner. The second premise mostly blocks that: almost all energy production damages the environment.

So look past energy. Energy is only one way that making a product can harm the environment. What about mining, logging, or drilling for the raw materials in the first place? What about the waste that goes to a landfill when nothing is recycled? Recycling could win on those counts even if energy is a tie.

The columnist treats one part of the environmental cost as if it were the whole cost. Two options that tie on one factor only tie overall if nothing else differs.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the columnist fails to consider environmental effects other than energy use. The best version would say recycling might help the environment in some way unrelated to energy. That would show the energy tie doesn't settle the overall comparison.

notes.body: Equivocation needs a key word to change meaning between premise and conclusion. Here "environment" means the same natural world throughout: energy production damages it, and making products damages it. The problem is that the columnist counts only one kind of damage, not that the word shifts.

B says the argument mixes up cause and effect. But the argument's only causal claim runs the normal way: energy production causes environmental damage. The columnist never treats the damage as a cause of energy use, so nothing is reversed.

C would fit if the columnist drew a conclusion about all recycled products from a few. But the conclusion is limited to "some types of products," the same products the premise is about ("those products"). The argument never generalizes, so representativeness isn't an issue.

This matches the prediction. The columnist compared the two options on one factor, energy, found a tie, and declared them tied overall. D names what got left out: making products from recycled materials "may have environmental benefits unrelated to energy consumption," such as less mining or logging, or less landfill waste.

Run the test for a "fails to consider" answer: it means ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. If recycling helps the environment in ways that have nothing to do with energy, then equal energy use doesn't make the two options equally damaging. The conclusion falls.

The move to repeat: when an argument compares two options on one factor and draws a conclusion about the whole, look for the answer naming another factor that could tip the balance.

E describes the post hoc flaw: one thing followed another, so the first caused the second. Nothing in the argument relies on timing or sequence. The claim that energy production damages the environment is stated as a general premise, and on Flaw questions we accept premises as true.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (probably)
old_steps.body: Making some stuff from recycled materials is probably as bad for the environment as it would be to make it from nonrecycled materials.

old_steps.label: Evidence (and)
old_steps.body: The recycling process uses as much energy as producing them from raw materials would, and almost all energy damages the environment.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Given that recycling uses as much energy as producing from scratch, how can we argue that making stuff from recycled materials is still better for the environment?
We could potentially argue that the energy we use to recycle is a more environmentally friendly energy than the style we use to make from scratch, but they're essentially blocking that avenue with the 2nd premise.
We should consider other parts of environmental impact besides just the energy supplied to the recycling / manufacturing machines. What about the impact of the raw materials? Of the distribution and transportation of the materials? Are there different chemical byproducts from the manufacturing process?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body:
The author is looking at only one component of a very complex net gain / net loss calculation.
She's assessing the overall environmental impact of recycled products vs. nonrecycled products, but she's only examining one slice of that comparison: energy involved to produce the product.
She's failing to consider all other ways in which the two different options might be asymmetric, in terms of environmental impact.

old_notes.body: Equivocation occurs when a key term is used with different meanings in different parts of the argument, creating the illusion of a valid inference. For this flaw to apply, the word "environment" would need to shift in meaning between premises and conclusion. But the argument uses "environment" and "environmental damage" consistently throughout — it just dramatically underestimates what that concept includes. The error is not that the meaning of the word changes; the error is that the argument fails to account for everything the word encompasses. This is a scope problem (ignoring relevant factors), not a semantic problem (changing word definitions). The argument has a single, consistent understanding of "environment" — it is just an impoverished one.

Treating an effect as a cause (or vice versa) involves confusing the direction of a causal relationship — like concluding that wet streets cause rain. The argument here makes no causal claims whatsoever between recycling and traditional manufacturing. The two processes are being compared side by side, not linked in any cause-and-effect sequence. The argument's structure is purely comparative: recycling and traditional manufacturing use the same amount of energy, therefore they cause similar environmental damage. The error is in the scope of that comparison (looking only at energy), not in any confusion about which process causes which outcome. There is simply no causal chain in this argument to reverse.

A sampling error occurs when a conclusion about a larger population is drawn from an unrepresentative subset — like surveying only cat owners about which pets are best. The argument here involves no sampling whatsoever. It does not survey some recycling operations and generalize to all of them. The argument's error is entirely conceptual: it equates energy consumption with total environmental impact. This scope error would persist even with perfect, comprehensive data covering every recycling and manufacturing operation on Earth. If you had flawless energy consumption figures for every factory in existence, the argument would still be wrong because it ignores non-energy environmental factors. The problem is the analytical framework, not the quality or representativeness of any sample.

The argument's reasoning chain is: recycling uses as much energy as traditional manufacturing, and energy production damages the environment, therefore recycling is probably as environmentally damaging as traditional manufacturing. This conclusion only follows if energy consumption is the sole determinant of environmental impact — an assumption that is plainly unjustified. Environmental impact is multi-dimensional. Recycling may reduce landfill overflow, decrease the need for raw material extraction (mining, logging, drilling), lower toxic waste output, reduce water pollution, preserve biodiversity by limiting habitat destruction, and conserve non-renewable resources. Two processes can consume identical amounts of energy while having vastly different environmental footprints across these other dimensions. The argument focused exclusively on energy and treated it as a proxy for total environmental impact, when in reality it is just one factor among many. This answer correctly identifies that failure: the argument ignores environmental benefits of recycling that have nothing to do with energy.

The correlation-versus-causation flaw occurs when someone observes that two phenomena co-occur and incorrectly concludes that one must cause the other. The argument here does not involve any correlation at all. It directly compares the energy consumption of two processes and draws a conclusion about their relative environmental impact. No one is claiming that recycling causes traditional manufacturing or vice versa, nor that energy use and environmental damage merely happen to coincide. The argument asserts a direct, reductive equivalence: same energy input means same environmental damage output. That is a scope error — treating one factor as the whole story — not a confusion about whether correlation implies causation. The flaw categories are entirely different.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: If we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Six months ago the city raised the fines for parking violations, to help pay for a parking garage that had just opened. Since then, parking violations on city streets have dropped by 50 percent.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
A common pattern in Logical Reasoning: "Policy X went into effect. Then Y happened. So X caused Y." The official assumes the higher fines caused the 50 percent drop. The conclusion depends on that causal story: "if we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again" only makes sense if fines are what reduced violations.

This is an Explain Curious Fact argument. Curious fact: violations dropped by half. The official's explanation: the higher fines. Alternate explanation: read the first sentence again. A new parking garage opened at the same time. Drivers who used to park illegally on the street may now have somewhere legal to park. That would cut violations whether or not the fines changed.

The official mentions the garage only as the reason the fines were raised, then forgets about it. That's the detail the test wants us to catch. When a stimulus mentions a second change at the same time, ask whether that change could explain the result.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer saying the official fails to rule out another cause for the drop. The best one names the obvious rival: the new garage gave drivers more legal places to park.

There's also a smaller worry. Even if the fines did cause the drop, raising them again may not add much. At some point the fine is already high enough: whether it's $500 or $600, I'm equally determined not to get that ticket. But the official only predicts "even fewer" violations, so this worry is weaker than the garage, which threatens the causal claim the whole recommendation rests on.

notes.body: A describes reversed causation: treating something that resulted from the drop as if it caused the drop. The fine increase came first, six months ago, and was made to help pay for the garage, not in response to fewer violations. Nothing here that came after the drop is being cast as its cause.

B is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a real worry: maybe a second raise won't work as well. But check what the official needs. The conclusion only says raising fines again would bring "even fewer" violations. Any further drop would do. Negate B: a second raise reduces violations less than the first did. The conclusion can still be true, so the argument doesn't take B for granted.

Compare that with E. If the garage caused the drop, the fines may do nothing at all, and the recommendation collapses.

The city's income from fines has nothing to do with whether higher fines reduce violations. The conclusion is about getting fewer violations, and money the city earns can't weaken a claim about how fines change drivers' behavior.

The official doesn't need illegal parkers to prefer parking legally. A higher fine can push people into legal spaces they dislike. Negate D: illegal parkers would rather keep parking illegally. Fines could still deter them, so the argument survives, which means D isn't something it assumes.

This is the alternate cause we predicted. The garage opened at the same time the fines went up, so either change could explain the 50 percent drop. If the drop came from the new parking spaces, raising fines again may do nothing, and the recommendation falls apart.

E's wording, "fails to establish," means the argument needed this and didn't prove it. To recommend higher fines, the official had to rule out the garage, and didn't.

The move to repeat: when an argument credits one change for a result, scan the stimulus for anything else that changed at the same time. The rival cause is often planted in a clause that reads like background, like "to help pay for the parking garage that had just opened."

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
old_steps.body: If we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Six months ago we raised the fines for parking violations, and since then parking violations on our streets have dropped by 50%.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
A common trope in Logical Reasoning is to say, "Policy change X went into effect. Then thing Y happened. So, apparently policy change X caused thing Y."
It seems here that our author is definitely making that same causal assumption, that the increase in fines is the cause of the 50% drop in parking violations.
The conclusion has implicit causality. When you say, "If you want X, you should do Y", you're implying that Y can bring about X.
This is the classic Explain Curious Fact argument structure, and when it shows up on Flaw, it means that they are usually just testing our awareness that the author has overconfidently arrived at one possible explanation for a curious fact, even though others could exist.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body:
So we might see answers saying, "The author takes for granted that because X was followed by Y, X caused Y" or "the author fails to consider other things could have caused there to be 50% fewer parking violations (a pandemic or storm that led to there being fewer people out and about, or maybe an increase in visibility of meter maids making people worry about whether they still had value left on their meter).
But there's also a prediction aspect to the conclusion, so even if we thought the fines were the causal reason that violations dropped by 50%, we won't necessarily get a further reduction by increasing fines even more. At a certain point, you've already maxed out the disincentive to get a parking violation. Whether it's a $500 or $600 fine, I'm equally determined to not get that ticket.

old_notes.body: Confusing cause and effect means reversing the causal direction — claiming X caused Y when actually Y caused X. The argument's timeline is straightforward and correct: fines were raised, then violations decreased. There is no reversal of the causal arrow. The actual flaw is different: the argument ignores a confounding variable (the parking garage) that could explain the same outcome. This is an alternative-cause error, not a reversed-causation error. The argument gets the temporal sequence right but fails to consider that another simultaneous change might be the real explanation. These are distinct logical errors, and this answer identifies the wrong one.

This answer identifies a real but secondary issue: diminishing returns. Perhaps the first fine increase captured the "easy wins" — the most price-sensitive violators — and a second increase would affect fewer people. But this critique is premature. The primary flaw is more fundamental: the argument has not established that fines caused the initial decrease at all. The parking garage is an unexamined alternative explanation. Before questioning whether a second dose of medicine will work as well as the first, we should first confirm the first dose was actually medicine and not a placebo. This answer skips ahead to a secondary objection while missing the foundational problem.

This answer introduces a cost-benefit analysis: do the revenues from fines justify the costs of enforcement? But the argument's conclusion is about effectiveness ("raise fines to reduce violations further"), not about profitability ("raise fines to make money"). The logical flaw lies in the causal reasoning — attributing the decrease in violations to fines while ignoring the garage. Whether fines are financially worthwhile is a completely separate question from whether they actually caused the behavioral change. This answer operates in the wrong analytical framework for a flaw question about causal reasoning.

This answer claims the flaw is assuming illegal parkers would prefer to park legally. But the argument's logic relies on deterrence through financial punishment, not on changing people's parking preferences. Deterrence works even when people prefer the illegal option — they choose the legal option to avoid the fine, not because they like it better. The argument does not need to assume anything about preferences; it only needs to assume fines change behavior through the threat of cost. The actual flaw is much simpler and more fundamental: the argument ignores that the new parking garage, not the fines, might explain the reduced violations.

This is the classic alternative-cause or confounding-variable flaw. Two events occurred simultaneously: the fine increase and the garage opening. Violations decreased by 50%. The argument attributes the decrease entirely to the fine increase and recommends a second increase. But it fails to consider that the parking garage — which provided new legal parking spaces — could be the actual explanation. People may have stopped parking illegally because they finally had a convenient legal option, not because they feared costlier tickets. Without controlling for this alternative cause, the argument's causal attribution is unjustified, and its recommendation (raise fines again) rests on an unproven foundation.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
At one Tuesday meeting, the club's president took a survey of all members present.
Of those surveyed, 95 percent said that they had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The club's president concluded that the attendance problem [at weekly meetings] was not due primarily to schedule conflicts.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Let's survey the customers at a sushi restaurant about whether they like fish. Or ask the people at a dog park whether dogs make good pets. We know what answer we'll get.

The president did the same thing. The survey went only to members present at a Tuesday meeting. Of course those people have no trouble attending on Tuesdays: they're there. The members most likely to have a Tuesday conflict are the ones who missed the meeting, and they never got a survey.

That matters because the attendance problem is about the people who don't come. The president drew a conclusion about why members miss meetings from the members who didn't miss this one. How many absent members stay home because Tuesday doesn't work for them? The survey can't tell us.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer describing a Sampling flaw: the president generalized from a sample that isn't representative of the group the conclusion is about. The answer might say it abstractly (an unrepresentative sample) or concretely (the survey left out members who couldn't attend on Tuesday).

notes.body: Circular reasoning means the premise already assumes the conclusion. Here the premise is a survey result and the conclusion is about why attendance is low. Those are different claims. The result was close to guaranteed by who was asked, which can feel circular, but that is a sampling problem, not a premise restating the conclusion.

This matches the prediction. In B, "a sample that is likely to be unrepresentative" is the members present at a Tuesday meeting. The phrase "making a generalization" is the conclusion about why the club has an attendance problem. The survey asked only the people who made it on a Tuesday whether Tuesday works for them, so the members with Tuesday conflicts were screened out by the way the survey was taken.

The move to repeat: whenever a conclusion rests on a survey, ask who got the survey and who didn't. If the method leaves out the very people the conclusion is about, the answer is a sampling flaw.

C is tempting because 95 percent is not 100 percent. But the president didn't treat the result as having no exceptions. The conclusion is that the problem was not due "primarily" to schedule conflicts, which allows for some conflicts. The flaw is who was surveyed, not how far the president stretched the number.

No two premises conflict. A survey was taken at a Tuesday meeting, and 95 percent of those surveyed had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays. Both can be true together. The premises are consistent; they just don't support the conclusion.

E describes a necessary vs. sufficient error about a change that won't solve a problem. The president never claims that moving the meeting wouldn't be enough to fix attendance and then infers it isn't needed. The argument runs from a survey to a conclusion about the cause, with no conditional reasoning at all.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body:
At one Tuesday meeting, the club's president took a survey of all members present.
Of those surveyed, 95 percent said that they had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: The club's president concluded that the attendance problem [at weekly meetings] was not due primarily to schedule conflicts.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
This sounds like a great approach. Let's go to a sushi restaurant and ask the customers if they like to eat fish. Or maybe we'll go to a dog park and ask the people there if dogs make good pets.
It's not surprising for people who are present at a Tuesday meeting to say that they have no problem attending on Tuesdays. But it's very possible that this selection of people are do not accurately represent the club members as a whole. And the president is making a conclusion about the club members as a whole.
How many club members did not answer the survey because they can't attend Tuesday meetings due to a schedule conflict? We don't know.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We'll expect a correct answer to describe a Sampling flaw.

old_notes.body: Circular reasoning occurs when the conclusion is restated as a premise — when the argument assumes the very thing it is trying to prove. The president's conclusion is that no members have significant conflicts with Tuesday. The premise is survey data from Tuesday attendees showing 95% reported no difficulty. These are technically distinct claims: one is about what a survey showed, the other is a generalization about the full membership. The problem is not that the conclusion sneaks into the premises but that the evidence was gathered from a biased source. It may feel circular because the result was essentially predetermined by the sampling method, but the logical structure is biased sampling, not circular reasoning. Circular reasoning involves no real evidence at all; the president's argument has evidence — it is just fatally skewed evidence.

The president surveyed members at a Tuesday meeting about whether they have difficulty attending on Tuesdays. The people present at a Tuesday meeting are, by definition, people who can attend on Tuesdays. Members who have significant scheduling conflicts with Tuesday are systematically excluded from the survey because they would not be at the meeting. This makes the sample fundamentally unrepresentative of the full membership. The 95% "no difficulty" result was practically guaranteed by the sampling method itself — asking only the people who successfully showed up whether showing up is hard for them. It is the equivalent of surveying marathon finishers about whether the race was too difficult and concluding it was easy for everyone. The people for whom it was genuinely too difficult never crossed the finish line and were never asked. The evidence tells us about the subset who can attend, but the conclusion claims to cover the entire membership.

This answer describes treating a generalization as if it has no exceptions — moving from "most" to "all" or ignoring outliers within a valid trend. While the president does make a sweeping claim about the entire membership, the fundamental problem occurs much earlier in the reasoning. The data itself is fatally biased because the wrong people were surveyed. Even if the president had softened the conclusion to "most members do not have conflicts" or "the vast majority are fine with Tuesday," the argument would still be deeply flawed because the data does not represent the full membership. You cannot fix a biased sample by being more careful about how you state the conclusion. The problem is at the evidence-gathering stage, not the conclusion-drawing stage.

Contradictory premises would mean the argument contains two claims that logically cannot both be true simultaneously. The president's premises — a survey was conducted at a Tuesday meeting and 95% of attendees reported no difficulty — are perfectly consistent with each other and with the conclusion. Nothing in the argument contradicts anything else within the argument. The problem is that internally consistent premises can still fail to support a conclusion when the evidence is gathered from a biased source. The premises get along fine; they just do not prove what the president thinks they prove. Internal consistency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a good argument. The evidence needs to actually be representative of the relevant population, and here it spectacularly is not.

Confusing sufficient and necessary conditions involves misunderstanding conditional relationships — like concluding "if the ground is wet, it rained" from "if it rains, the ground is wet." The president's argument contains no conditional reasoning of any kind. There is no "if X, then Y" structure being inverted or misapplied. The argument is entirely about evidence gathering and generalization: a survey was conducted, results were obtained, and a conclusion was drawn. The flaw lies in who was included in the survey (only Tuesday attendees), creating a systematically biased sample. This is a data collection error, not a formal logic error about the relationship between conditions. Diagnosing a necessary/sufficient confusion here applies the wrong diagnostic framework to the wrong category of problem.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: If the proposed measures are adopted, we'll spend about a billion dollars less on ozone-related health costs.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
If the proposed measures are adopted, ozone levels in the city's air will be one fifth lower than they are now.
Ozone is currently responsible for over $5 billion in health costs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author takes one fifth of the $5 billion in ozone health costs and assumes that cutting ozone by one fifth cuts those costs by one fifth.

But who said the relationship is one to one? Given that ozone will drop by a fifth, how could we argue the costs won't drop by a billion?

Maybe health costs depend on a threshold. Suppose ozone makes people sick only above a certain level, and even 80 percent of today's ozone is well above it. Then cutting ozone by a fifth might barely change health costs. Or it could run the other way: the last fifth of the ozone could be the most harmful part, and the savings could be bigger than a billion.

Either way, the argument needs costs to rise and fall in step with ozone levels, and it never shows that.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying "just because ozone is reduced by one fifth doesn't mean ozone-related health costs will be reduced by one fifth." In flaw language: the author presumes, without evidence, that health costs are proportional to ozone levels.

notes.body: Check the conclusion's exact words: we would spend less on "these ozone-related health costs." If other pollutants rose, other health costs would rise, not ozone-related ones. So A attacks a claim about total health costs that the author never made.

This names the assumption we predicted. The author got from $5 billion to about $1 billion by taking one fifth, which only works if ozone-related health costs vary "roughly in proportion to ozone levels." The argument offers no evidence for that. If costs only kick in above some threshold, a one fifth cut in ozone could save far less than a fifth of the costs.

Run the test for a "presumes" answer: negate it and see if the argument survives. Health costs don't vary in proportion to ozone? Then the billion-dollar figure has no support. So the argument depends on B.

The move to repeat: when an argument turns a percentage change in one thing into the same percentage change in another, look for a proportionality assumption.

The conclusion is conditional: we would save the money "should the proposed measures be adopted." It never claims the measures will be adopted, so it owes us no reason to think they will be. C criticizes the argument for not proving something it never claimed.
The argument contains no appeal to emotion. It runs on numbers: a one fifth reduction, over $5 billion, about a billion. The flaw is in that math, not in an attempt to stir up feelings.

E accuses the author of a motive: using air pollution to distract from bigger health costs. Nothing in the argument suggests a hidden purpose. The topic is ozone-related costs, and the argument stays on it. The error is a bad assumption about those costs, not a change of subject.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: If the proposed air pollution measures are adopted, it will save us about $1 billion in health costs.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body:
If the proposed air pollution measures are adopted, ozone levels will be 1/5 what they currently are.
The ozone in our air currently costs us over $5 billion in health costs.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The author is taking 1/5 of the $5+ billion price tag of ozone health costs and assuming that if we reduce ozone by 1/5, then we reduce those costs by 1/5.
But who said it would be a 1:1 ratio of ozone-reduction to cost-reduction? Maybe 80% of our current ozone (1/5 less) is functionally the same as 100% of our current ozone levels.
Perhaps most of the health care costs kick in when even 20% of the current ozone levels are present. Maybe once ozone passes a certain threshold, we rack up health costs, and any additional ozone in the air after that point adds negligible additional costs.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer saying "just because ozone is reduced by 1/5 doesn't mean associated health costs will be reduced by 1/5".

old_notes.body: This answer suggests the flaw is failing to consider that other types of pollution might increase to compensate for ozone reduction. While that is a legitimate real-world concern, it does not identify the actual logical flaw in the argument's reasoning. The argument's error is mathematical, not environmental: it assumes that a one-fifth reduction in ozone levels translates directly to a one-fifth reduction in ozone-related health costs. This proportionality assumption would be flawed even if no other pollutants existed. The relationship between ozone concentration and health outcomes could be exponential, could involve threshold effects, or could follow any number of non-linear patterns. Pointing to other pollutants addresses a secondary, external concern while missing the glaring proportionality assumption at the argument's core.

The argument's structure is: ozone-related health costs total $5 billion; if ozone were one-fifth lower, health costs would decrease by one-fifth, saving $1 billion. This arithmetic only works if health costs scale in direct, linear proportion to ozone concentration levels — an assumption the argument makes without any justification. But dose-response relationships in environmental health are typically non-linear. Threshold effects are common: ozone may be relatively harmless below a certain concentration but severely damaging above it. Alternatively, there may be diminishing marginal effects at lower concentrations or accelerating damage at higher ones. A 20% reduction in ozone could produce anywhere from negligible savings to a dramatic drop in health costs, depending on where on the dose-response curve current levels fall. The argument treats a complex epidemiological relationship as simple division. This answer correctly identifies that unjustified proportionality assumption as the core flaw.

This answer points to a practical concern: perhaps the proposed measures to reduce ozone will never actually be implemented. While that is a legitimate real-world worry about policy feasibility, it is not a logical flaw in the argument's reasoning structure. The argument makes a conditional claim: IF ozone levels were one-fifth lower, THEN health costs would drop by about $1 billion. The logical flaw is in the "then" part — the assumed proportionality between ozone reduction and cost reduction. Whether the "if" part actually happens is a separate question about political or practical feasibility, not about the soundness of the reasoning. Even if the ozone-reducing measures were guaranteed to be adopted, the proportionality assumption would still be unjustified. This answer identifies an implementation obstacle rather than a reasoning error.

An appeal to emotions substitutes emotional persuasion for logical reasoning — using fear, sympathy, outrage, or other feelings instead of evidence and analysis. The argument here does the opposite: it relies entirely on numerical data and mathematical calculation. It cites $5 billion in costs, a one-fifth reduction in ozone, and computes $1 billion in savings. This is about as clinical and quantitative as an argument can get. The flaw is not that the argument appeals to feelings but that its quantitative reasoning contains an unjustified mathematical assumption — specifically, that health costs scale proportionally with ozone levels. The argument is too reliant on numbers, not too reliant on emotions; it just gets the numerical relationship wrong.

Drawing attention away from a more significant issue (a red herring) involves introducing an irrelevant topic to distract from the real subject under discussion. The argument here stays squarely focused on ozone and health costs throughout. Every element of the argument — ozone levels, health cost figures, the proposed reduction, the projected savings — directly pertains to its central claim. There is no digression, no attempt to change the subject, and no irrelevant tangent introduced to distract from a more important source of pollution. The argument is focused but wrong: it maintains laser precision on the topic while embedding a flawed mathematical assumption in its reasoning. Staying on topic and being right are two different things, and this argument achieves the first while failing at the second.
